resolution_table.mechanism: Grain sorghum competes with HRW for southern-Plains acreage and feed/export demand, with ambiguous flat-price effect via relative returns.
resolution_table.blurb: Grain sorghum and wheat compete for acreage and demand, creating unclear price effects.

resolution_table.mechanism: KC hard red winter and MATIF milling wheat are the two milling-grade origins that bid against each other in MENA and Asian tenders. AUTHOR-ON-STRUCTURE: 3 co-mention props, complex:wheat / group:food_grains, slice Jaccard 0.679 -- the missing MATIF-KC link.
resolution_table.blurb: KC and MATIF milling grades bid against each other in the same MENA and Asian tenders.

resolution_table.mechanism: Palm and soybean oil are close substitutes in the global edible-oil pool; a high soyoil price lifts palm demand and the whole vegoil complex moves together.
resolution_table.blurb: Soyoil scarcity and high costs shift biodiesel demand to palm, raising its price.

resolution_table.mechanism: Palm competes with soyoil for biodiesel feedstock share; tight soyoil/RBD economics pull discretionary biodiesel toward palm, supporting price.
resolution_table.blurb: Soyoil scarcity and high costs shift biodiesel demand to palm, raising its price.

resolution_table.mechanism: South American/US soybean crush volumes set soyoil supply, the dominant palm substitute, so soybean S&D propagates into the vegoil complex including CPO.
resolution_table.blurb: Soybean crush volumes drive soyoil supply, which substitutes for palm oil across vegetable oils

resolution_table.mechanism: Rapeseed/canola oil is a substitute in EU food and biodiesel demand; canola tightness raises palm's call as a replacement vegoil.
resolution_table.blurb: Canola scarcity increases demand for palm oil as alternative vegetable oil.

resolution_table.mechanism: Black Sea sunflower oil availability shifts the substitution pool; sunoil shortfalls (e.g. war disruption) divert demand to palm.
resolution_table.blurb: Black Sea sunflower oil disruption diverts demand toward palm oil substitutes.

resolution_table.mechanism: CPO is the feedstock the refiner fractionates into olein, so DCE olein offtake and the refining margin over CPO pull physical crude palm out of the Malaysian balance -- 132 co-mention props at lift 32.27, the estate's strongest measured pair.
resolution_table.blurb: CPO fractionates into olein, so olein offtake and refining margin pull crude palm out of the balance.

resolution_table.mechanism: One fresh fruit bunch yields both mesocarp CPO and the kernel that is crushed into PKO and PKM, so kernel output and the lauric price move with the same milled tonnage that sets CPO supply -- 194 co-mention props at lift 4.87.
resolution_table.blurb: One fruit bunch yields both CPO and the kernel, so kernel output moves with milled tonnage.

resolution_table.mechanism: Soybean oil is the closest substitute for palm olein in Chinese food use; a high soyoil price shifts demand to olein and lifts DCE prices alongside the vegoil complex.
resolution_table.blurb: High soybean oil prices shift Chinese food demand toward palm olein, raising its prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Palm olein competes with soyoil for biodiesel and food blending share; tight soyoil economics pull discretionary demand toward palm, supporting olein.
resolution_table.blurb: High soybean oil prices shift Chinese food demand toward palm olein, raising its prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Chinese and South American soybean crush sets domestic soyoil supply, the dominant olein substitute, so soybean S&D propagates into DCE olein pricing.
resolution_table.blurb: Soybean crush from China and South America determines domestic soyoil supply, the primary olein substitute, driving olein prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Rapeseed/canola oil is a substitute in Chinese cooking-oil demand; rapeseed tightness raises the call on palm olein as a replacement, lifting DCE price.
resolution_table.blurb: Rapeseed tightness shifts demand to palm olein, raising prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Olein is CPO plus a refining and freight margin, so the DCE olein board cannot move independently of the Malaysian crude palm price it is fractionated from -- 132 co-mention props at lift 32.27.
resolution_table.blurb: Olein is CPO plus refining and freight margin, so it cannot move independently of crude palm.

resolution_table.mechanism: Soybean meal is the dominant feed protein and the direct substitute for RSM; higher soymeal prices pull Chinese feed demand toward RSM and lift ZCE RSM prices.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher soybean meal prices shift Chinese feed demand toward rapeseed meal, raising its prices

resolution_table.mechanism: Soybeans are crushed into the soymeal that competes with RSM; a tight/expensive soybean balance sheet raises soymeal and drags RSM higher through the protein complex.
resolution_table.blurb: Tight soybean supplies raise soymeal prices, pulling rapeseed meal higher through protein competition

resolution_table.mechanism: Rapeseed oil is the co-product of the same crush; firm rapeseed oil demand keeps crushers running and conditions the meal byproduct economics behind RSM.
resolution_table.blurb: Rapeseed oil demand drives crushing operations, improving meal byproduct economics.

resolution_table.mechanism: ICE canola (Canadian rapeseed) is the dominant imported feedstock for Chinese crush; higher canola seed prices raise the cost basis of domestically produced RSM.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher canola prices raise costs for domestic rapeseed meal production in China.

resolution_table.mechanism: Corn is the energy component paired with protein meal in compound feed; cheaper corn can raise total feed rations (more meal) while expensive corn squeezes inclusion budgets, ambiguous net effect on RSM.
resolution_table.blurb: Cheaper corn allows more protein meal in feed; expensive corn limits meal inclusion, net effect unclear.

resolution_table.mechanism: Palm oil is the dominant imported edible oil in China and sets the floor of the vegetable-oil complex; higher palm prices pull rapeseed oil higher via substitution in food/blending.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher palm oil prices raise rapeseed oil prices through food and blending substitution.

resolution_table.mechanism: Soybean oil is the largest-volume Chinese edible oil; rising DCE soyoil prices lift rapeseed oil as close cooking-oil substitutes and narrow the rape-soy oil spread.
resolution_table.blurb: Abundant soyoil from high crush and imports captures cooking-oil share, pressuring rapeseed oil.

resolution_table.mechanism: Imported soybeans crushed in China compete with rapeseed in the oilseed complex; a tight/expensive soybean balance drags rapeseed oil higher through oil substitution.
resolution_table.blurb: Tight soybean supplies push rapeseed oil prices higher as crushers switch oilseeds.

resolution_table.mechanism: A cheap, abundant soyoil supply (high crush, big soybean imports) captures cooking-oil share and pressures rapeseed oil via oil-share competition.
resolution_table.blurb: Abundant soyoil from high crush and imports captures cooking-oil share, pressuring rapeseed oil.

resolution_table.mechanism: Raw and white (refined) sugar are tightly linked via the white premium (refining margin); a strong white premium incentivizes refiners to buy raws, pulling raw price up, and the two move together as substitutes for end demand.
resolution_table.blurb: Strong refining margins incentivize refiners to buy raw sugar, pulling raw prices up alongside white sugar.

resolution_table.mechanism: Sugarcane is split between sugar and ethanol; when ethanol economics dominate, mills divert cane to ethanol, reducing raw sugar supply and lifting raw sugar price (the dominant Brazilian cross-product competition).
resolution_table.blurb: Ethanol demand surge diverts sugarcane from sugar production, tightening raw sugar supply and raising price.

resolution_table.mechanism: In Brazil, corn ethanol expansion can substitute for cane ethanol at the margin, freeing cane for sugar; conversely high corn prices favor cane ethanol, indirectly linking sugar mix decisions to corn economics.
resolution_table.blurb: High corn prices shift cane toward ethanol, reducing sugar output; low corn prices free cane for sugar production.

resolution_table.mechanism: HFCS substitutes for sugar in beverages and processed food -- Mexican bottlers won injunctions to substitute HFCS in place of sugar, and Mexico's HFCS tax existed to defend its sugar industry (Tier 2, corpus-narrated); cheap corn sweetener caps sugar's industrial demand.
resolution_table.blurb: Cheap HFCS displaces sugar in beverages, capping industrial sugar demand and price.

resolution_table.mechanism: Robusta substitutes for arabica in roaster blends and instant coffee; when arabica is dear, demand and price support flow to robusta, while a robusta supply shock can also pull arabica higher as the two compete for blend share.
resolution_table.blurb: Arabica and robusta compete in blends; high arabica prices boost robusta demand and prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: US rice competes with corn for Mid-South acreage and water; relative returns shift planted area between them.
resolution_table.blurb: Rice and corn compete for Mid-South acreage and water; returns determine which farmers plant.

resolution_table.mechanism: In food and feed use, wheat and rice are partial caloric substitutes; sharp wheat moves can spill into rice demand and policy responses.
resolution_table.blurb: Wheat price spikes shift demand to rice, triggering policy responses in rice markets.

resolution_table.mechanism: Soybeans compete with rice for US Mid-South acreage, influencing rice plantings via relative profitability.
resolution_table.blurb: Soybean profitability relative to rice affects US Mid-South rice planting decisions.

resolution_table.mechanism: Wheat and corn compete for feed-ration demand and acreage; higher corn prices pull feed wheat demand and raise the wheat-corn spread floor, supporting SRW.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher corn prices increase wheat demand and support soft red winter wheat prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Soybeans compete with wheat for double-crop and fall acreage decisions in the SRW belt, with ambiguous flat-price effect via relative returns.
resolution_table.blurb: Soybeans and wheat compete for acreage; relative returns drive planting choices.

resolution_table.mechanism: SRW and KC HRW are protein grades of one crop -- mills blend across the KC-CBOT spread, so an HRW supply shock reprices SRW through the blend ladder (Tier 1, reciprocal of the incumbent kcbt edge).
resolution_table.blurb: Mills blend across the KC-CBOT spread, so HRW tightness reprices soft red winter.

resolution_table.mechanism: SRW and MGEX HRS share the global wheat balance sheet; the protein premium widens on spring-wheat tightness and SRW is the discount leg of the same blend (Tier 1, reciprocal of the incumbent mgex edge).
resolution_table.blurb: SRW is the discount leg of the protein ladder spring wheat tops; the spread links them.

resolution_table.mechanism: CBOT SRW and MATIF milling wheat are the two export benchmarks for soft and standard milling wheat; the Gulf-Rouen spread reallocates destination demand (Tier 1, reciprocal of the incumbent matif edge).
resolution_table.blurb: The Gulf-Rouen spread reallocates export demand between CBOT and MATIF wheat.

resolution_table.mechanism: JSE white maize is arbitraged against CBOT/yellow corn through import and export parity; the global corn benchmark sets the ZAR-converted parity band that bounds local price.
resolution_table.blurb: Global corn benchmark converts to local currency, setting local maize price boundaries

resolution_table.mechanism: Cheap feed wheat substitutes for yellow maize in livestock rations, indirectly easing maize demand and the white-yellow premium when wheat is price-competitive.
resolution_table.blurb: Cheap feed wheat substitutes for maize in livestock rations, easing maize demand and white-yellow premium.

resolution_table.mechanism: Maize competes with soybeans and sunflower for South African summer-crop hectares; relative gross margins reallocate planted area between them.
resolution_table.blurb: Maize, soybeans, sunflower compete for land; better margins shift planting between crops.

resolution_table.mechanism: SAFEX yellow maize is tethered to CBOT corn through import/export parity; CBOT corn leads SAFEX flat price (adjusted for rand and freight) in both deficit and surplus regimes.
resolution_table.blurb: CBOT corn leads South African yellow maize prices through import-export parity adjustments.

resolution_table.mechanism: Yellow and white maize compete for the same SA planted area and share weather; the white-yellow spread reallocates acreage and signals relative demand (white for human meal, yellow for feed).
resolution_table.blurb: White maize demand signals shift planted acreage from yellow maize for feed use.

resolution_table.mechanism: Cheap feed wheat substitutes for yellow maize in SA poultry/feedlot rations when the wheat-maize spread compresses, easing maize feed demand.
resolution_table.blurb: Cheaper feed wheat replaces maize in poultry feed when price gap narrows, reducing maize demand.

resolution_table.mechanism: Soybeans compete with maize for summer-crop area on the Highveld; the soy/maize gross-margin ratio reallocates planted hectares between them.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher soybean-to-maize profit ratio shifts planting from maize toward soybeans.

resolution_table.mechanism: Soybean meal is a direct crush product of soybeans; higher bean prices raise raw-material cost and floor meal price, and bean supply shocks pass through to crushable meal availability.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher soybean prices raise soybean meal costs; supply shocks reduce meal availability.

resolution_table.mechanism: Meal and oil are joint crush products competing for crush value; when soyoil value rises (oil share up), processors capture margin from oil and sell meal aggressively, pressuring meal price.
resolution_table.blurb: Rising soybean oil value shifts processor focus away from meal, increasing meal supply pressure.

resolution_table.mechanism: Corn is the energy component paired with meal protein in feed rations; higher corn prices raise total ration cost and can shift formulation, while corn acreage competition with soybeans tightens crushable bean supply for meal.
resolution_table.blurb: High corn prices increase feed costs and reduce soybean acreage, tightening meal supply.

resolution_table.mechanism: Rapeseed/canola meal substitutes for soymeal in feed rations; a higher rapemeal price shifts protein demand toward soymeal, firming meal demand and price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher rapeseed meal price shifts protein demand toward soybean meal, raising soybean meal demand and price.

resolution_table.mechanism: Distillers grains are the corn-ethanol co-product that displaces soymeal on relative protein value in the feed ration, so DDGS availability and price set part of the marginal meal ton -- 113 co-mention props at lift 3.16.
resolution_table.blurb: Distillers grains displace soymeal on relative protein value, setting part of the marginal meal ton.

resolution_table.mechanism: Soybeans are crushed into meal; a higher imported soybean cost directly raises the input cost of DCE meal and lifts its price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher imported soybean cost raises domestic meal input costs and prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Meal and oil split the value of each crushed bean; when soybean oil commands a higher share of crush value, processors discount meal to clear it, pressuring meal price.
resolution_table.blurb: Oil's higher crush value share forces processors to discount meal, pressuring meal prices downward.

resolution_table.mechanism: Corn and meal are joint inputs in Chinese hog/poultry feed rations; a higher corn price raises energy-feed cost and increases protein (meal) inclusion in least-cost rations, supporting meal demand and price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher corn price increases meal's share in feed rations, supporting meal demand and price.

resolution_table.mechanism: Rapeseed/canola meal substitutes for soybean meal in feed; a higher rapemeal price shifts ration demand toward soymeal, firming DCE meal price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher canola meal price shifts feed demand toward soybean meal, firming soybean price.

resolution_table.mechanism: Palm oil substitutes for soybean oil; a higher palm price lifts soyoil value and oil_share of crush, letting crushers discount meal to move it, a mild bearish channel for meal.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher palm prices increase soybean oil value, letting crushers discount meal to sell it faster.

resolution_table.mechanism: Distillers grains sit in China's MARA soymeal-reduction basket beside rapeseed and cottonseed meal, so DDGS import availability moves the marginal protein ton on the DCE board -- 113 co-mention props at lift 3.16.
resolution_table.blurb: DDGS sits in China's MARA soymeal-reduction basket, moving the marginal protein ton.

resolution_table.mechanism: Palm oil is the largest substitute for soyoil in food frying and biodiesel; a higher palm price (e.g. Indonesia/Malaysia supply shock or export ban) shifts demand to soyoil, raising soyoil price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher palm oil prices shift demand to soybean oil, raising its price

resolution_table.mechanism: Sunflower oil competes with soyoil in food use; a Black Sea sunoil supply shock raises sunoil prices and diverts demand to soyoil, lifting its price.
resolution_table.blurb: Black Sea supply shock raises sunflower oil prices, shifting demand to soybean oil and raising its price.

resolution_table.mechanism: Rapeseed/canola oil competes in food and especially EU biodiesel; a higher rapeseed-oil price shifts vegoil and biofuel demand toward soyoil, supporting its price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher rapeseed oil prices shift food and biodiesel demand toward soybean oil, raising its price.

resolution_table.mechanism: Soybeans are the raw feedstock crushed into soyoil; higher bean prices raise soyoil input costs (bullish) but also reflect more crush throughput that lifts soyoil output (bearish), so the net pass-through depends on oil share.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher soybean prices increase soyoil input costs but also boost output; net effect depends on oil's margin share.

resolution_table.mechanism: Soyoil and meal are joint products of the same crush; strong meal demand drives crush and co-produces more soyoil, weighing on soyoil price, while weak meal demand throws relative value to oil.
resolution_table.blurb: Strong meal demand increases crush volume, raising soyoil supply and lowering soyoil price

resolution_table.mechanism: Corn competes with soybeans for US spring acreage; higher corn prices pull acres from soy, reducing future bean (and thus soyoil) supply and supporting soyoil price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher corn prices reduce soybean acreage, tightening soybean supply and raising soyoil prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Beef tallow competes with soyoil for renewable-diesel and biodiesel capacity -- an official feedstock pair on EPA RFS pathways and CARB LCFS CI tables (Tier 1), and corpus-narrated (Paraguayan producers opt for tallow over soy oil; Brazil runs ~80% soyoil with tallow the remainder).
resolution_table.blurb: Tallow and soyoil bid for the same renewable-diesel capacity, linking their prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: UCO is the lowest-CI competing feedstock for the same renewable-diesel capacity soyoil feeds -- official on RFS/LCFS/45Z (Tier 1) and corpus-narrated (Tidewater's RD slate names UCO, tallow, canola and soybean oil; Canadian biodiesel blends UCO with soybean oil).
resolution_table.blurb: UCO competes with soyoil for renewable-diesel demand, capping soyoil's share of capacity.

resolution_table.mechanism: Palm oil is the primary substitute for soyoil in Chinese food and biodiesel; a higher palm price shifts demand to soyoil and lifts DCE soyoil price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher palm prices shift Chinese demand to soybean oil, lifting its price

resolution_table.mechanism: Rapeseed/canola oil competes with soyoil in Chinese cooking-oil blends; a higher rapeoil price (e.g. canola tariffs) diverts demand to soyoil, supporting DCE price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher canola prices shift Chinese cooking-oil demand to soybean oil, supporting prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Soyoil is jointly produced from crushing imported soybeans; higher bean cost raises crush feedstock value and the floor under DCE soyoil price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher soybean import costs raise crushing feedstock value and establish price floor for soyoil.

resolution_table.mechanism: Oil and meal share the crush value; weak meal demand shifts the crush burden onto oil so processors must extract more value from soyoil, supporting its price.
resolution_table.blurb: Weak meal demand shifts crush burden to oil, supporting soyoil prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Soybeans and corn compete for the same spring acreage; a higher corn price pulls acres away from soybeans, tightening soy supply and raising soy price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher corn price shifts spring planting toward corn, tightening soybean supply and raising soybean price.

resolution_table.mechanism: Strong soybean meal demand (feed) lifts crush margins and pulls bean demand forward, supporting soybean price.
resolution_table.blurb: Soybean meal demand for feed lifts crush margins and pulls soybean prices higher.

resolution_table.mechanism: Robust soybean oil demand from biodiesel and food lifts crush economics and bean demand, supporting price.
resolution_table.blurb: High biodiesel and food demand strengthens crush economics, lifting soybean prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Palm oil substitutes for soybean oil in food and fuel; a higher palm price shifts demand to soyoil, raising crush value and bean price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher palm price shifts demand to soybean oil, raising soybean crush value and price.

resolution_table.mechanism: Sunflower oil competes with soyoil in food and biodiesel; a higher sunoil price (e.g. Black Sea supply shock) shifts demand to soyoil, lifting crush value and bean price.
resolution_table.blurb: Black Sea supply shock raises sunflower oil prices, shifting demand to soybean oil and raising bean prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Rapeseed/canola oil competes in food and biodiesel; a higher rapeseed-oil price shifts vegoil demand toward soyoil, supporting crush and bean price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher rapeseed-oil price shifts food demand toward soyoil, raising soybean crush and bean price.

resolution_table.mechanism: Rapeseed/canola meal competes with soybean meal in feed rations; a higher rapemeal price firms soymeal demand and crush pull, supporting bean price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher rapeseed meal price increases soybean meal demand, supporting soybean prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Soybeans and corn compete for the same US spring acreage; a higher corn price pulls acres away from soybeans, tightening soy supply and raising soy price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher corn price reduces soybean acreage, tightening supply and raising soybean price.

resolution_table.mechanism: Strong soybean meal feed demand lifts crush margins and pulls bean demand forward, supporting soybean price.
resolution_table.blurb: Soybean meal demand rises, improving crush margins and increasing soybean purchases, lifting prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Robust soybean oil demand from biodiesel/renewable diesel and food lifts crush economics and bean demand, supporting price.
resolution_table.blurb: Strong biodiesel and food demand boost crush margins and soybean prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Palm oil substitutes for soybean oil in food and fuel; a higher palm price shifts demand to soyoil, raising crush value and bean price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher palm price shifts demand to soybean oil, raising soybean price.

resolution_table.mechanism: Sunflower oil competes with soyoil in food/biodiesel; a higher sunoil price (Black Sea shock) shifts demand to soyoil, lifting crush value and bean price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher sunflower oil prices shift demand to soybean oil, raising soybean crush value and prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Rapeseed/canola oil competes in food and biodiesel; a higher rapeoil price shifts vegoil demand toward soyoil, supporting crush and bean price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher rapeseed oil price shifts food demand to soybean oil, supporting soybean crush and prices

resolution_table.mechanism: Rapeseed/canola meal competes with soybean meal in feed rations; a higher rapemeal price firms soymeal demand and crush pull, supporting bean price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher rapeseed meal price increases soybean meal demand, supporting soybean prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Soybeans and corn compete for the same Northeast China spring acreage; higher corn prices (or stronger corn subsidies) pull acres away from non-GMO soybeans, tightening domestic supply and raising DCE No.1 price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher corn prices reduce soybean acreage, tightening supply and raising soybean futures prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Imported GMO beans (No.2) crushed for oil/meal can substitute non-GMO beans at the margin in lower-value uses; cheap No.2 caps the No.1 food-grade premium and pressures No.1 price.
resolution_table.blurb: Cheap imported crushed beans cap food-grade premiums and pressure prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Domestic meal demand mainly pulls imported No.2 beans through the crush; only a weak residual linkage to food-grade No.1 beans exists, so the effect on No.1 price is ambiguous.
resolution_table.blurb: Meal demand drives imported No.2 bean crush; weak spillover to No.1 bean prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Soybeans and corn compete for the same origin spring acreage; a higher corn price pulls acres away from soybeans, tightening the future exportable surplus to China and raising imported-bean price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher corn prices shift spring acreage away from soybeans, tightening export supply and raising imported soybean prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Strong Chinese soybean meal feed demand lifts domestic crush margins and pulls imported-bean demand forward, supporting DCE No.2 price.
resolution_table.blurb: Chinese feed demand strengthens crush margins and boosts imported soybean demand, supporting prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Robust Chinese soybean oil demand from food and biodiesel lifts crush economics and imported-bean demand, supporting price.
resolution_table.blurb: Chinese soybean oil demand from food and biodiesel strengthens crush margins and imported bean demand, lifting prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Palm oil substitutes for soyoil in Chinese food use; a higher palm price shifts demand to soyoil, raising crush value and imported-bean demand.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher palm price shifts Chinese food demand to soybean oil, raising crush values and bean imports.

resolution_table.mechanism: Rapeseed/canola meal competes with soybean meal in Chinese feed rations; a higher rapemeal price firms soymeal demand and crush pull, supporting imported-bean price.
resolution_table.blurb: Higher rapeseed meal price strengthens soybean meal demand and crush margins, supporting imported bean prices.

resolution_table.mechanism: Palm olein and sunoil are the two interchangeable bottled oils in the Indian and Middle East retail pack, so the palm-sunoil spread is what reallocates that demand -- 111 co-mention props / 220 doc, lift 4.74, npmi 0.165 on the post-X2 corpus.
resolution_table.blurb: Palm and sunoil are interchangeable bottled oils; the spread reallocates Indian retail demand.

resolution_table.mechanism: Sunoil and soyoil substitute in food use inside the vegetable-oil complex (Tier 1, the estate's ratified transmission family); a tight soyoil balance diverts food demand to sunoil, and the incumbent edges assert the same mechanism the other way.
resolution_table.blurb: Tight soyoil supplies divert food demand to sunflower oil, lifting its price.

resolution_table.mechanism: White (#5) and raw (#11) sugar are joined by the white premium (refining margin); the #5 = raw cost + refining value, so the two move together and the spread (white premium) is the key relative-value lever — a richer raw market lifts the #5 base.
resolution_table.blurb: Raw sugar costs drive white sugar prices; refining margin adjusts the spread between them.

resolution_table.mechanism: Cane is split between sugar and ethanol; when ethanol economics dominate in Brazil/India, mills divert cane to fuel, reducing raw feedstock for refining and lifting white sugar.
resolution_table.blurb: Ethanol demand in Brazil and India diverts cane from sugar refining, reducing white sugar supply.

resolution_table.mechanism: Corn ethanol expansion in Brazil can free cane for sugar at the margin, while high corn prices favor cane ethanol; corn economics thus indirectly shape the cane sugar mix feeding refineries.
resolution_table.blurb: Corn prices influence how much sugarcane gets directed to ethanol versus sugar production.

resolution_table.mechanism: HFCS substitutes for refined sugar in beverages and processed food -- the Mexican sweetener wars (bottler injunctions, the HFCS tax as sugar-industry leverage) are corpus-narrated Tier-2 receipts; cheap corn sweetener caps white sugar's industrial demand.
resolution_table.blurb: HFCS displaces refined sugar in beverages, capping white sugar industrial demand.

inverted_pairs_all.mechanism: Robusta substitutes for arabica in roaster blends and instant coffee; when arabica is dear, demand and price support flow to robusta, while a robusta supply shock can also pull arabica higher as the two compete for blend share.
inverted_pairs_all.blurb: Arabica and robusta compete in blends; high arabica prices boost robusta demand and prices.

inverted_pairs_all.mechanism: Feed barley substitutes for corn in rations, particularly in EU and Black Sea, when price-competitive.
inverted_pairs_all.blurb: Barley replaces corn in livestock feed when prices favor barley in EU and Black Sea regions.

inverted_pairs_all.mechanism: Feed barley substitutes for corn in rations, particularly in EU and Black Sea, when price-competitive.
inverted_pairs_all.blurb: Barley replaces corn in livestock feed when prices become competitive

inverted_pairs_all.mechanism: Feed barley substitutes for maize in EU and Black Sea rations when price-competitive, easing maize demand.
inverted_pairs_all.blurb: Barley substitutes for maize in feed when price-competitive, reducing maize demand.

inverted_pairs_all.mechanism: Canadian canola is the same oilseed at the same crush yield and lands into the EU crush and biodiesel book MATIF prices, so the two are one substitution pair rather than two markets -- 203 co-mention props at lift 6.61, slice Jaccard 0.677.
inverted_pairs_all.blurb: Canadian canola is the same oilseed and lands into the EU crush book MATIF prices.

inverted_pairs_all.mechanism: Rapeseed/canola oil is a substitute in EU food and biodiesel demand; canola tightness raises palm's call as a replacement vegoil.
inverted_pairs_all.blurb: Canola scarcity increases demand for palm oil as alternative vegetable oil.

inverted_pairs_all.mechanism: ICE canola (Canadian rapeseed) is the dominant imported feedstock for Chinese crush; higher canola seed prices raise the cost basis of domestically produced RSM.
inverted_pairs_all.blurb: Higher canola prices raise costs for domestic rapeseed meal production in China.

inverted_pairs_all.mechanism: Corn-oil and the broader biofuel feedstock complex compete for renewable-diesel demand; corn/ethanol economics indirectly influence vegetable-oil pull on canola.
inverted_pairs_all.blurb: Corn oil and vegetable oils compete for renewable diesel demand, affecting canola prices.

inverted_pairs_all.mechanism: Corn competes with cotton for US/Brazil/India planting area; a higher cotton-to-corn new-crop price ratio pulls acreage to cotton, raising future corn-relative cotton supply.
inverted_pairs_all.blurb: Higher cotton prices shift plantings from corn to cotton, reducing future corn supply.

inverted_pairs_all.mechanism: MATIF maize is arbitraged against CBOT corn via import parity; the US board sets the global flat-price anchor that EU maize follows after FX.
